item.title: Case Study: French Kitchenware Brand Cut Aluminum Utensil Costs by 32%
item.description: This is the full playbook of a real engagement we closed for CuisinePro — a French kitchenware importer with 11 distributors across the EU. Six months ago they were locked into a Guangzhou trading company paying €2.68 per aluminum utensil with a 38% QC reject rate. Today they source directly from a Chaozhou factory at €1.82, with 4% defects, LFGB §31 + CE compliant, privately labeled, and landed DDP Le Havre in 28 days. Every number in this post comes from signed invoices, AQL inspection reports we attended on-site, and our client’s landed-cost ledgers — no estimates, no rounding.

item.title: Supplier Relationship Management China: Tiering Incentives & Risk Diversification
item.description:
Most China buyers treat suppliers as disposable: find the cheapest one place an order repeat until something breaks then find a new one. This transactional approach costs more in the long run — in re-audit expenses quality failures stockouts and lost negotiation leverage.

Supplier Relationship Management (SRM) is the opposite approach: treating your supplier base as a strategic portfolio to be tiered incentivized and diversified. This guide covers the 4-tier supplier classification system the 3 incentive mechanisms that actually work with Chinese factories the risk diversification strategies (single dual and multi-source) and the 5 long-term benefits of building real partnerships. We include a real case study of a client who reduced supply disruption risk by 18% by transitioning from single-source to dual-source.

item.title: China Supplier Evaluation Scorecard: 10-Dimensional Factory Rating Template
item.description:
Every buyer who has sourced from China has faced the same question: “I have 5 quotes. The prices range from 2.10 to 3.80 USD. Which factory do I pick?” Most buyers pick the cheapest one and hope. The smarter ones pick the middle one and pray. The professional buyers use a supplier evaluation scorecard — a structured 10-dimensional rating system that removes emotion and guesswork from the decision.

This guide gives you the complete scorecard we use at Yeatru for every factory evaluation. Each of the 10 dimensions is scored 0–10 with clear scoring criteria you can apply yourself. We include a real case study of a 2026 engagement where we scored 5 factories for a US kitchenware brand and selected the winner — and why the cheapest factory scored dead last. We also describe the downloadable template format so you can replicate it in your own procurement process.

item.title: Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR) for Chinese Factories: Template & Process
item.description:
What Is a Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR)?

A Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR) is a formal, documented request that a supplier investigate the root cause of a defect and change its process so the defect cannot recur. It sits inside the wider CAPA system (Corrective and Preventive Action): the corrective action fixes the specific batch, and the preventive action changes the process permanently. A SCAR is triggered when a defect is critical, when a defect rate breaches your AQL 2.5 major standard, or when the same defect reappears across batches — precisely when a one-off rework has already proven insufficient.

item.title: Purchase Order Process China Sourcing: From PO Issue to Delivery SOP
item.description:
A purchase order is the most important document in China sourcing. It is the contract that defines what you are buying how much you pay when it ships and what happens if something goes wrong. Yet 71% of first-time buyers issue a one-line PO (“10 000 pcs silicone spatula at 0.85 USD”) and wonder why the factory delivered a different product.

This guide walks you through the complete 8-step purchase order process that Yeatru uses for every client engagement. Each step includes a checklist and the most common pitfalls. We include a real case study of a 12 000 USD order from PO signature to delivery a payment method comparison and a list of 10 mandatory clauses that every China PO must contain.

item.title: Product Category Sourcing Guide China: Electronics Home Apparel Toys Beauty Outdoor
item.description: Sourcing from China without category-specific knowledge is like trying to buy a car from a grocery store — the product exists somewhere on the shelves but the staff cannot tell you which one fits your spec which one is safe and which one will break in 3 months. Every major product category in China has its own geographic cluster its own supply-chain rituals its own certification burden and its own set of scams.

item.title: How to Read a China Inspection Report: Sections, Red Flags & How to Challenge It
item.description:
What Is a China Inspection Report?

A China inspection report is the written record a QC inspector produces after physically sampling a production lot at the factory, usually during a pre-shipment inspection (PSI). It states the lot size, the sample size (n) drawn under ISO 2859-1 / ANSI Z1.4, the AQL levels (default 2.5 major / 4.0 minor / 0 critical), the defect count in each class, the accept (Ac) versus reject (Re) comparison, dated photo evidence, and a final Pass / Conditional / Fail verdict. It is a contract deliverable that releases or withholds your balance payment — not a marketing PDF.

item.title: FOB vs CIF from China: Which Saves You Money?
item.description:
What Are FOB and CIF?

FOB (Free On Board) and CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) are both sea-freight Incoterms where the seller delivers goods onto the vessel at the port of shipment. Under both, risk transfers when the goods are on board. The difference is who pays for the ocean freight and cargo insurance:

item.title: FOB Origin vs FOB Destination: Who Pays Freight & Who Bears Risk
item.description:
What Are FOB Origin and FOB Destination?

FOB Origin and FOB Destination are US domestic shipping terms used in B2B commerce within the United States. They determine who pays the freight carrier and when title (ownership) and risk of loss transfer between buyer and seller. Despite sharing the “FOB” acronym, these are not the same as the Incoterms FOB used for international sea freight.

item.title: FCA vs FOB for China Sourcing: When to Use Each
item.description:
What Are FCA and FOB?

FCA (Free Carrier) and FOB (Free On Board) both require the seller to clear goods for export and deliver them to a carrier, with the buyer paying international freight, insurance, import duty, and last-mile. The difference is the type of carrier and the legal point of risk transfer:

item.title: FCA vs EXW for China Sourcing: Which to Use & Why
item.description:
What Are FCA and EXW?

EXW (Ex Works) is the Incoterm that places maximum obligation on the buyer. The seller only needs to make the goods available at their factory or warehouse; you arrange and pay for everything from that point: China inland trucking, export clearance, international freight, insurance, import clearance, duty, and last-mile.

item.title: How to Get Factory Direct Pricing in China: Avoid Trading Company Markups
item.description: Every China buyer has seen the price gap: the same silicone spatula quoted at 2.80 USD by one supplier and 4.20 USD by another for the identical spec. The 1.40 USD difference is not quality — it is the trading company markup. The 2.80 USD quote came from the actual Ningbo silicone factory; the 4.20 USD quote came from a Yiwu trading company that buys from that same factory and marks it up.

item.title: ETA vs ETD in China Shipping: What Each Date Means
item.description:
What Do ETA and ETD Mean?

ETD (Estimated Time of Departure) is the date and time a vessel or aircraft is scheduled to leave the origin port or airport — for China sourcing, that means leaving a Chinese port such as Ningbo, Shanghai or Shenzhen (or an airport such as Guangzhou or Hong Kong). ETA (Estimated Time of Arrival) is the date and time it is scheduled to reach the destination port or airport. The two are linked: the carrier calculates the ETA by adding its published transit time to the ETD.

item.title: Eco Regulations China Sourcing: CSRD, CBAM, EU Battery, Prop 65
item.description:
What Are Eco Regulations?

Eco (environmental) regulations are laws that impose environmental obligations on products, their supply chains, or the companies that sell them. Unlike voluntary eco certifications, these are mandatory — non-compliance leads to customs refusal, fines, or product recalls. For China importers, the regulations that matter most are in the destination market (EU and US), but China’s own environmental enforcement also affects factory availability and cost. The key regulations are EU CBAM (carbon border tax), EU CSRD (sustainability reporting), EU Battery Regulation (battery passport), EU Packaging Regulation (recycled content), California Prop 65 (chemical warnings), US TSCA (chemical substances), and China’s dual carbon goals. See also product certifications and eco certifications.

item.title: Eco Certifications China: ISO 14001, FSC, GOTS, GRS
item.description:
What Are Eco Certifications?

Eco (environmental) certifications are third-party-verified labels that prove a product or factory meets environmental standards — responsible forestry, organic fibres, recycled content, chemical safety, energy efficiency, or carbon neutrality. When you source from China, eco certifications matter for three reasons: market access (Amazon, Walmart, EU public procurement require them), brand protection (greenwashing claims need evidence), and regulatory compliance (EU CSRD, CBAM and EPR schemes create mandatory disclosure duties). The most relevant standards for China importers are ISO 14001 (factory environmental management), FSC (wood/paper), GOTS (organic textiles), GRS (recycled content), OEKO-TEX (textile chemicals), EPEAT and Energy Star (electronics). See also product certifications and ethical sourcing.

item.title: Defective Goods from China: Claim, Rework, Replacement & Refund Playbook
item.description:
What Is a Defective-Goods Claim Against a Chinese Supplier?

A defective-goods claim is a formal, documented demand that a Chinese supplier remedy goods that fail your agreed specification after delivery. It is built on three things: evidence taken before the goods are sorted or resold, a defect rate measured against the contract’s AQL 2.5 major / 4.0 minor / 0 critical standard, and a written remedy (rework, replacement, refund or price credit) within the contract’s claim window. A claim is not a complaint — it is a contract action with a number attached.

item.title: DDU vs DDP for China Sourcing: The Difference & Who Pays Duty
item.description:
What Does DDU Mean, and How Does It Differ From DDP?

DDU (Delivered Duty Unpaid) and DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) are both door-to-door shipping arrangements. Under either one the seller arranges export clearance in China, international freight, insurance, and delivery to the buyer’s address. The one difference is import customs clearance and import duty: with DDU the buyer clears customs and pays the duty; with DDP the seller does both.

item.title: DAP vs DDP for China Sourcing: Key Differences & Cost
item.description:
What Are DAP and DDP?

DAP (Delivered at Place) and DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) are the two Incoterms 2020 terms where the seller delivers goods all the way to the buyer’s door. The seller handles export clearance, international freight, insurance, and last-mile delivery. The only difference is who handles import clearance and pays import duty: under DAP it’s the buyer; under DDP it’s the seller.

item.title: CIF vs CIP for China Sourcing: Insurance, Risk & Mode
item.description:
What Are CIF and CIP?

CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) and CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To) are the two Incoterms where the seller pays for both freight and cargo insurance to the destination. The key difference is transport mode:

  • CIF applies to sea and inland waterway transport only. The seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port. Risk transfers when goods are on board the vessel at the port of shipment.
  • CIP applies to any mode of transport (air, sea, road, rail, multimodal). The seller pays freight and insurance to the named destination. Risk transfers when goods are handed to the first carrier.

Think of CIP as the all-modes version of CIF. CIP is the correct term when the journey isn’t purely sea — for example, Yiwu → Shenzhen truck → Hong Kong air → EU, or China → Europe by rail.

item.title: China Procurement Cost Breakdown: The True TCO Beyond Unit Price
item.description:
Most first-time China buyers build their sourcing budget on a single number: the factory’s unit price. They multiply by quantity add a rough guess for freight and call it done. Then the container arrives and the actual invoice is 25–40% higher than expected. The difference is not fraud — it is the cost components that the factory quote deliberately does not include.

This guide breaks down the 6 cost components that make up the true total cost of ownership (TCO) for a China-sourced order: product unit price tooling/sampling certification/testing quality control logistics/freight and duties/taxes. For each component we give the percentage range real dollar amounts and the common traps that inflate it. We close with a full cost breakdown of a real 5 000 USD PO and a comparison table showing how a unit-price-only decision differs from a TCO-based decision.

item.title: China Buying Agent: What It Is, Fees & How to Choose
item.description:
What Is a China Buying Agent?

A China buying agent is a buyer-side professional who sources products from Chinese suppliers on your behalf: finding and vetting factories, negotiating price and terms, running quality inspections, preparing export documents and coordinating freight. The same role is described in different industries as a procurement agent, purchasing agent, manufacturing sourcing agent or simply a sourcing agent — the label changes, the function does not. Critically, a buying agent works for the buyer and is paid a disclosed fee, while a trading company buys and resells goods on its own account and hides its margin in the price.

item.title: Market Research Before Sourcing from China for the US
item.description:
What This Article Is About

Every month, aspiring US importers message us with the same request: “Find me a product with good margins, low MOQ, and US market potential.” It is a reasonable ambition, but it is the wrong starting point. A China-based sourcing partner can tell you what is manufacturable, what the factory price is, and what the MOQ will be — but we cannot decide what you should sell. That decision depends entirely on US-side market research: the retail price the market will bear, how many competitors already hold the category, what your customer acquisition cost will be, and whether the product fits your budget. This article explains the research you must complete first, why trending products are usually a trap, and how to narrow a broad category down to one specific, sourceable item. It is the honest prerequisite to FBA product research and to any first-time China sourcing effort.

item.title: Yiwu Sourcing Agent for UK Buyers: Import from China to UK
item.description: UK buyers sourcing from Yiwu face a thicker compliance layer post-Brexit: UKCA marking replaces CE on the GB market, UK-REACH regulates SVHC in imported articles, and a GB EORI is mandatory on every customs declaration. A Yiwu sourcing agent for UK buyers closes that gap end-to-end — supplier verification, UKCA-aligned spec, AQL 2.5 QC, export declaration, DDP shipping to Felixstowe, and Postponed VAT Accounting setup. This guide breaks down the UK-specific rules, costs, ports, and a worked example for a typical £20,000 kitchenware order.

item.title: Yiwu Market Sourcing Guide 2026: 75,000+ Suppliers
item.description:
What Is the Yiwu Market?

The Yiwu International Trade City (义乌国际商贸城, Yiwu International Trade Mart) in Yiwu, Zhejiang is the world’s largest wholesale market for small commodities — a permanent, indoor complex covering 7.5 million sqm across 5 districts, with 75,000+ booths selling 2.1 million+ SKUs across toys, hardware, kitchenware, jewelry, electronics, garments, and imported goods. Unlike 1688.com (online B2B) or the Canton Fair (twice-yearly), Yiwu is open daily year-round and built for walk-in cash-and-carry wholesale: a buyer can source 200 SKUs from 60 booths, pay 50% deposits, and have everything consolidated and shipped within 3 weeks. It is the default destination for Amazon FBA sellers, dollar-store chains, and TikTok Shop creators running low-MOQ mixed-category orders.

item.title: Yiwu Agent for Foreigners: How to Source from Yiwu
item.description:
What Is a Yiwu Agent for Foreigners?

A Yiwu agent (义乌采购代理) is a Yiwu-based, locally-licensed sourcing and export company that represents a foreign buyer end-to-end: booth tours and translation at the International Trade City, supplier and booth verification on gsxt.gov.cn, price negotiation, sample management, AQL 2.5 pre-shipment QC, consolidation warehousing, export declaration through their licensed 代理报关 entity, FX conversion, and DDP shipping to the buyer’s door. Foreign individuals cannot legally register an export declaration or claim the China VAT export refund on their own — that is why the export-agent piece is structural, not optional. A genuine Yiwu agent works for the buyer (transparent commission, discloses the booth); a Yiwu trading company works for itself (marks up, hides the booth) — see sourcing agent vs trading company.

item.title: XTransfer for China Sourcing: Cross-Border Payment Guide
item.description:
What Is XTransfer?

XTransfer is a cross-border B2B payment platform built specifically for China trade. It gives Chinese suppliers virtual receiving accounts in major currencies (USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, HKD) that behave like local bank accounts. Instead of sending an international SWIFT wire (which stacks sender, intermediary, and recipient bank fees), a buyer sends a local transfer (ACH in the US, SEPA in the EU, Faster Payments in the UK) to the supplier’s virtual local account. XTransfer then converts the funds to RMB at a competitive rate and pays the supplier’s Chinese bank account. It is regulated for cross-border payments and runs KYC/compliance checks on every supplier account. See how it fits into the broader landscape in how to pay Chinese suppliers safely.

item.title: What Is a China Sourcing Agent? Roles, Fees & Services
item.description:
What Is a China Sourcing Agent?

A China sourcing agent is an independent, buyer-side intermediary that manages the entire China-to-door purchasing pipeline on your behalf for a transparent fee. Unlike a trading company (which buys, owns, and resells goods at a markup) or Alibaba (a self-service marketplace where you deal with suppliers directly), an agent never takes title to your goods. It finds the real factory, verifies it, negotiates price, runs quality control, and ships DDP — answering to you, not the supplier.

item.title: How to Verify a Chinese Supplier License (Free Tool)
item.description:
What Is Business License Verification?

Business license verification is the process of checking a Chinese supplier’s 营业执照 (business license) against the official government registry at gsxt.gov.cn (National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System, run by the State Administration for Market Regulation, SAMR). The license image the supplier sends you is just a piece of paper — it can be Photoshopped, borrowed from another company, or revoked since issuance. The gsxt.gov.cn record is the live truth: current registration status, abnormal-operations flags, administrative penalties, and annual report filings. This is the single cheapest, highest-leverage due-diligence step before any deposit; pair it with a factory audit and the 50/50 deposit rule for full protection.

item.title: UKCA Marking from China: Post-Brexit Compliance Guide (2026)
item.description:
What Is UKCA Marking?

UKCA — UK Conformity Assessed — is the United Kingdom’s product conformity marking introduced after Brexit to replace the EU’s CE mark for products placed on the Great Britain market (England, Wales, and Scotland). UKCA is the manufacturer’s self-declaration (or, for higher-risk products, a UK Approved Body’s verified confirmation) that the product meets the applicable UK regulations. The technical requirements are nearly identical to the EU directives — UKCA uses UK-adopted designated standards (the BS EN versions of the same harmonized standards) — but the documentation, the responsible person, and the mark itself must be UK-specific. Northern Ireland is treated separately under the Windsor Framework and continues to accept CE marking. UKCA is enforced by UK Trading Standards and the Health and Safety Executive at the border and through post-market surveillance.

item.title: Alibaba Trade Assurance Explained: Does It Protect Buyers?
item.description:
What Is Alibaba Trade Assurance?

Alibaba Trade Assurance (TA) is Alibaba’s buyer-protection program for orders placed on Alibaba.com. Instead of paying the supplier directly, the buyer pays into Alibaba’s protected account. Alibaba holds the funds and releases them to the supplier only after the order is shipped and the buyer confirms receipt, or after the agreed inspection conditions are met. If the supplier fails to ship, ships goods that do not match the agreed specification, or ships the wrong quantity, the buyer can open a dispute and Alibaba mediates a refund from the held funds. It is the closest thing to true escrow in the Alibaba ecosystem and the safest way to pay on the platform. For orders off Alibaba, see the alternatives in how to pay Chinese suppliers safely.

item.title: How to Track a Shipment from China: Tracking Guide
item.description:
What Does “Tracking a China Shipment” Really Mean?

Tracking a China shipment means following a cargo’s status from the moment it leaves your supplier’s factory through export customs, the international leg (air or sea), destination import customs, and final delivery. Each mode — express, air, sea — uses a different tracking number format and a different tracking system, so the first step in any trace is identifying which number you have. The supplier, freight forwarder, and destination carrier each see only a slice of the journey; your job is to stitch those slices together and spot stalls early.

item.title: TikTok Shop Wholesale China: Bulk Sourcing for Resellers
item.description:
What Is TikTok Shop Wholesale Sourcing?

TikTok Shop wholesale sourcing is the practice of buying products in bulk from China — typically 500 to 5,000 pieces — at a discounted unit price, holding that inventory yourself (usually in a US 3PL or FBP warehouse), and reselling the units on TikTok Shop. Unlike dropshipping, where a third party ships each order, wholesale means you control the product, the packaging, and the fulfillment. The trade-off is inventory risk: a slower-moving SKU ties up capital. But for TikTok sellers scaling past the test-order stage, wholesale delivers meaningfully lower unit cost and higher gross margin than dropshipping, making it the default model for brands that want to compound profit.

item.title: TikTok Shop Sourcing from China: Low MOQ Guide
item.description:
What Is Sourcing for TikTok Shop from China?

Sourcing for TikTok Shop from China is the end-to-end process of finding, sampling, ordering, and shipping products that will sell on TikTok’s video-driven marketplace. It differs from Amazon sourcing in three ways: speed matters more than lowest price (trends die in weeks), MOQ must be low (you test before you scale), and the product must be visually demo-friendly (it has to look good in a 15-second video). The typical flow takes a product from idea to listed in 2–4 weeks, using small air-freighted test orders and fast-responding Chinese suppliers.

item.title: TikTok Shop Trending Products to Source from China (2026)
item.description:
What Are TikTok Shop Product Trends?

TikTok Shop product trends are the fast-rising product categories driven by short-form video virality — a product can go from zero to thousands of daily sales in days when a single creator video hits. Unlike Amazon search-driven demand, TikTok demand is visual and impulse-driven, so winning products tend to be small, lightweight, low-cost, and visually satisfying to demo. For sellers sourcing from China, the playbook is: spot the trend early, source a small batch at low MOQ, ship by air, test with video content, and scale fast — all within a typical 2–8 week trend window.

item.title: Fast Shipping for TikTok Shop from China: 3-7 Day Delivery
item.description:
What Is TikTok Shop Fast Shipping?

TikTok Shop fast shipping is the fulfillment speed requirement that separates sellers who win the Buy Box and the Fast Delivery badge from those who lose ranking and sales. TikTok’s algorithm rewards listings that ship quickly and reliably because viral trends create a short purchase window — usually 1–3 weeks. A product that takes 25 days to arrive is dead on arrival, because the trend has moved on before the buyer receives it. For sellers sourcing from China, this means choosing air-based modes (air freight, express courier, or DDP air) over sea freight, and keeping buffer stock in a US warehouse so orders can ship the same day.

item.title: TikTok Shop Compliance 2026: Product Requirements
item.description:
What Is TikTok Shop Compliance?

TikTok Shop compliance is the set of rules every seller must follow to list, ship, and sell on the platform in 2026 — covering prohibited products, required safety certificates, mandatory labeling, fulfillment speed (FBP/FBM), return policy, and seller account health metrics. Unlike a general marketplace, TikTok enforces these rules actively through automated scans and manual review because a single unsafe or counterfeit listing can go viral and damage buyer trust. For sellers sourcing from China, compliance starts at the factory: the product, its packaging, and its documentation must be correct before the first unit ships, because TikTok and US CBP both inspect on the way in.

item.title: Third-Party Inspection in China: SGS, BV, TUV
item.description: When sourcing from China, you have three independent inspection options: the big-4 third-party inspection (TPI) companies — SGS, Bureau Veritas (BV), TUV, and Intertek — mid-tier inspection firms, and sourcing-agent QC. Each tier has a different price point, report style, and best-fit use case. This guide compares all three, shows real 2026 cost ranges, explains letter-of-credit (LC) required inspection, and helps you decide which tier to book for each order.

item.title: China Sourcing Returns: Handling Defective Goods
item.description:
What Is a Defect Policy in China Sourcing?

A defect (or return) policy is the set of rules and contract clauses that govern what happens when goods from a Chinese supplier fail to meet your quality standard. Because returning goods to China is almost always more expensive than the product itself, the goal is not to send goods back — it is to negotiate rework, replacement, or a discount using evidence and contract leverage. A well-structured defect policy combines clear defect classification, remedy options, contractual protection, and a fast response process.

item.title: China Sourcing Prep Checklist Before Contacting Suppliers
item.description:
What Is Sourcing Preparation?

Sourcing preparation is the work you do before sending the first message to a Chinese supplier: defining the product, budget, volume, compliance, and logistics so the supplier can quote accurately. Suppliers receive 20-50 RFQs per day; vague requests get a generic high price or no reply, while a complete, professional RFQ gets fast, accurate quotes and signals you are a serious buyer. Preparation also protects you from the most common China-sourcing losses — wrong product, wrong MOQ, missing certifications, and surprise landed costs.

item.title: Sourcing Agent vs Direct Factory China: 2026 Comparison
item.description:
Direct Factory vs Sourcing Agent

Buying direct from a Chinese factory means contracting the manufacturer itself, with no trading company or agent in between — appealing because you skip the middleman markup. A sourcing agent sits between you and the factory, charging 5-8% to handle verification, negotiation, QC, export docs, and consolidation. The catch: most “direct” factories buyers find on Alibaba are trading companies, and genuine direct access requires Canton Fair visits, factory-region travel, or an agent’s introductions. The real question is not which is cheaper on unit price, but which is cheaper on total landed cost including your time and risk.

item.title: Sourcing Agent vs Buying Office: Which Is Better?
item.description:
Sourcing Agent vs Buying Office: The Core Difference

A sourcing agent is an independent, external company that manages your China sourcing pipeline for a transparent 5-8% commission — it works for you but is not your employee. A buying office is your own in-house entity in China: you register a WOFE, rent an office, hire local sourcing/QC/logistics staff, and pay them salaries. The agent is variable-cost and fast to start; the office is fixed-cost and slow to set up but gives you 100% control over pricing, suppliers, and IP. The decision hinges on your annual China sourcing volume and how much control you need.

item.title: China Sourcing Agent for USA Buyers: DDP to America
item.description:
China Sourcing for US Buyers

China sourcing for US buyers means buying goods from Chinese factories and clearing them through US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) — a process shaped by Section 301 tariffs (7.5–25% on top of MFN duty), US import fees (Merchandise Processing Fee 0.3464%, Harbor Maintenance Fee 0.125%), and US product compliance (CPSC, FCC, FDA). A US-aware China sourcing agent translates factory capability into US-compliant, customs-cleared shipments, handling HS-code classification, compliance verification, Amazon FBA prep, and DDP delivery to US warehouses or FBA centers.

item.title: Sourcing Agent for UAE & Saudi Arabia (GCC) Buyers
item.description:
China Sourcing for Middle East & GCC Buyers

China sourcing for Middle Eastern and GCC buyers means buying goods from Chinese factories and clearing them through the Gulf Cooperation Council markets (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain) — shaped by low duties (0–5%), GCC VAT (5–15%), mandatory product certification (SASO, ESMA, QCC, G-Mark), halal certification for food and cosmetics, and Arabic labeling. Dubai’s Jebel Ali port and free zone serve as the region’s re-export hub. A GCC-aware China sourcing agent handles certification verification, halal documentation, Arabic label translation, DDP shipping to GCC ports, and VAT-inclusive landed-cost modeling.

item.title: China Sourcing Agent for Latin America (Brazil, Mexico)
item.description:
China Sourcing for Latin American Buyers

China sourcing for Latin American buyers means buying goods from Chinese factories and clearing them through the complex customs and tax regimes of LATAM — shaped by high and layered taxes (Brazil’s IPI+ICMS stack of 60–100%), mandatory certification (INMETRO in Brazil, NOM in Mexico), Portuguese/Spanish documentation, and currency controls in Argentina and Brazil. A LATAM-aware China sourcing agent handles certification verification, certified translations, currency management, DDP shipping to major LATAM ports, and the full tax-stack landed-cost model.

item.title: China Sourcing Agent for Japan & Korea Buyers
item.description:
What Is China Sourcing for Japan & Korea Buyers?

China is the largest manufacturing supplier to both Japan and Korea, but sourcing for these two markets is more demanding than selling to the US or EU. Japan enforces some of the world’s strictest product safety and cosmetic-quality standards (PSE, METI, JIS, Food Sanitation Law), while Korea runs its own certification regime (KC, KCC, MFDS). Both markets also expect local-currency invoicing (JPY/KRW) and near-zero-defect quality. A China sourcing agent that specializes in Japan and Korea handles certification filing, quality matching, local invoicing, and port routing — turning a compliance minefield into a manageable pipeline.

item.title: China Sourcing Agent Fees 2026: 5-8% Commission
item.description:
What Are China Sourcing Agent Fees?

A sourcing agent fee is the compensation a buyer-side intermediary charges for managing the China-to-door purchasing pipeline — supplier discovery, factory verification, price negotiation, quality control, export documentation, and DDP logistics. Unlike a trading company that embeds a 10-30% markup into the unit price, a sourcing agent charges a visible, negotiated fee and discloses the real factory. The right fee model depends on your order size, frequency, and product complexity — picking the wrong one can cost you 2-5% of order value unnecessarily.

item.title: China Sourcing Agent for Canadian Buyers
item.description:
China Sourcing for Canadian Buyers

China sourcing for Canadian buyers means buying goods from Chinese factories and clearing them through the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) — a process shaped by Canadian customs (BN import account, HS-code MFN duty), GST/HST (5% federal plus provincial HST of 13–15% in participating provinces), and Canada product compliance (SOR/2016-174 consumer product safety, Health Canada, ISED for electronics). A Canada-aware China sourcing agent handles BN guidance, compliance verification, GST/HST modeling, DDP/DAP logistics, and port routing to Vancouver, Montreal, or Toronto.

item.title: China Sourcing Agent for Australia & New Zealand
item.description:
China Sourcing for Australian Buyers

China sourcing for Australian buyers means buying goods from Chinese factories and clearing them through the Australian Border Force (ABF) — a process shaped by GST of 10% on all imports, Australian Consumer Law (ACL) mandatory safety standards, the RCM (Regulatory Compliance Mark) for electronics, and strict biosecurity rules (ISPM 15 wood packaging, BICON permits for timber and plants). An Australia-aware China sourcing agent handles ABN guidance, compliance verification, GST modeling, biosecurity checks, DDP/DAP logistics, and port routing to Sydney, Melbourne, or Brisbane.
